---
title: "Cross-sectional dependence: how much, and of what kind"
subtitle: "Theory note 01 — the exponent α and the unordered tests"
---

> **Code:** [the exponent α](../panel-spat.qmd#sec-csd-exponent) for α and the
> routing, [testing for CSD](../panel-spat.qmd#sec-csd-tests) for the CD
> family. Spatial-structure tests are
> [theory note 03](03-spatial-dependence-tests.qmd).

## The two questions people confuse

Units move together. Almost always, in almost every panel. So "is there
cross-sectional dependence?" is nearly never the useful question — with a large
*N*, even an average pairwise correlation of 0.02 will reject.

The two questions that actually matter are different:

1. **Is the co-movement pervasive?** — does it involve a growing *share* of units,
   or a sparse, local handful? → this is **α**.
2. **Does it have geographic structure?** — is unit *i* correlated with its
   *neighbours* specifically? → this is the *ordered* family,
   [theory note 03](03-spatial-dependence-tests.qmd).

α answers the first. Everything in this note either measures it or is a coarse
test whose validity is *defined in terms of it*.

## 1. What α counts

Take a factor model where only *some* units load on the common shock:

$$z_{it} = a_i + \gamma_i f_t + \varepsilon_{it}, \qquad
  \#\{i : \gamma_i \neq 0\} = O(N^{\alpha}).$$

α is the growth rate of the **number of connected units**. That is the whole idea;
everything else is consequence.

| α | Units sharing the shock | Picture |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | a fixed *fraction* of *N* | an oil price shock — everyone feels it |
| 3/4 | grows, but the *share* vanishes | a regional bloc that widens slower than the panel |
| 1/2 | about $\sqrt{N}$ | sparse, local — a spatial weight matrix with bounded row sums |

Averaging is how you see it. For the cross-section average $\bar z_t$
[@bailey2016; @pesaran2015, eq. 29.6, p. 754]:

$$\operatorname{Var}(\bar z_t) = \underbrace{\kappa_0 N^{2(\alpha-1)}}_{\text{co-movement}}
  + \underbrace{\kappa_1 N^{-1}}_{\text{what independence gives}}
  + O(N^{\alpha-2}), \qquad \tfrac12 < \alpha \le 1.$$

The second term is the textbook $\sigma^2/N$. The first is the *excess* over it.
Two readings fall straight out:

- **α = 1** → $N^{0}$ → the excess never shrinks. Pooling more units never removes
  the common movement. This is **strong dependence**: common factors
  [@pesaran2015, p. 754].
- **α < 1** → the excess vanishes as $N \to \infty$. Formally **weak dependence**,
  which is where essentially all spatial models live
  [@pesaran2015, pp. 756, 802].

::: {.callout-note}
**Why the range is 1/2 < α ≤ 1.** Below 1/2 the $\kappa_1 N^{-1}$ term dominates
the $\kappa_0 N^{2(\alpha-1)}$ term, and α is no longer identified from the
variance of the average — sparse dependence is simply indistinguishable from
independence at the aggregate level. The restriction is not a technicality; it
says *there is nothing left to measure* down there.
:::

## 2. Reading α: the effective sample size

The label "weak" is asymptotic and can badly mislead in a finite panel. Set
$\kappa_0 N^{2(\alpha-1)} = \sigma^2/N_{\text{eff}}$ and you get the number that
actually matters — how many *independent* observations your *N* units are worth:

$$N_{\text{eff}} \;\propto\; N^{2(1-\alpha)}$$

| α | N = 100 | N = 1 000 | N = 9 000 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1.00 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 0.90 | 2.5 | 4.0 | 6.2 |
| 0.75 | 10 | 32 | 95 |
| 0.50 | 100 | 1 000 | 9 000 |

Read the α = 0.90 row slowly. Nine thousand individuals carry about as much
cross-sectional information as **six** independent ones, and going from 1 000 to
9 000 units bought you two. Yet α = 0.90 is formally "weak dependence", and a
great many published panels sit near it — @bailey2016 find most macroeconomic
series in roughly the 0.77–0.92 range, with equity returns essentially at 1.

**So: the weak/strong dichotomy is a limit theorem. α is the finite-sample truth.**
That gap is the entire reason to estimate it.

## 3. What α does *not* tell you

This is the easiest thing to get backwards, so state it plainly.

α says **nothing** about whether you need fixed effects. FE absorbs the
*time-invariant* unobserved heterogeneity $a_i$, and you need it for exactly the
reasons you always did. What α governs is a **different omitted variable**: the
*time-varying* common factor $f_t$ with *heterogeneous* loadings $\gamma_i$.

The identity that makes this click:

> **Two-way fixed effects is already a factor model — with $\gamma_i = 1$ for
> everyone.** A common time effect $\delta_t$ absorbs a common shock only if every
> unit responds by the same amount.

So heterogeneous loadings are precisely the case two-way FE cannot remove, and
α ≈ 1 is precisely where they bite. The correct summary:

::: {.callout-important}
**α does not tell you whether you need FE. It tells you whether FE is *enough*.**

- **Low α** → FE is *sufficient*. The omitted common shock, such as it is, washes
  out. Fix the standard errors and move on.
- **High α** → FE is *insufficient*. $f_t$ survives the within transformation, and
  if it correlates with your regressors the estimator is **biased, not merely
  inefficient**. No standard-error correction rescues a biased point estimate —
  not Driscoll–Kraay, not clustering, not spatial HAC. You need CCE
  [@pesaran2006], explained in [theory note 04](04-common-factors-cce.qmd), or
  interactive fixed effects.
:::

## 4. The CD test

Pesaran's CD [@pesaran2004; @pesaran2015, eq. 29.76, p. 786] is the average
pairwise residual correlation, scaled:

$$CD = \sqrt{\frac{2T}{N(N-1)}} \sum_{i<j} \hat\rho_{ij}
  \;\xrightarrow{d}\; N(0,1).$$

Two design choices explain everything about its behaviour.

**It sums raw $\hat\rho$, not $\hat\rho^{\,2}$.** The Breusch–Pagan LM statistic
[@breusch1980; @baltagi2021, p. 412] sums $T\hat\rho_{ij}^{\,2}$ into a $\chi^2$,
which needs $T \gg N$ — with large *N* you are accumulating $N(N-1)/2$ strictly
positive terms and it diverges. CD is *exactly* centred at zero under the null for
**any** *T*, because $E(\hat\rho_{ij}) = 0$ in finite samples and not merely
asymptotically. **That is its virtue: small T, enormous N, still valid.**

**Signed summation is also its fatal flaw**, in two specific ways:

- **Sign cancellation.** Dependence whose pairwise correlations average to zero is
  invisible, however strong each individual pair. Positive and negative spatial
  weights are the obvious case.
- **Demeaned residuals are dead on arrival.** Two-way FE forces
  $\sum_i \hat e_{it} = 0$, which drives $\bar\rho$ to roughly $-1/(N-1) \approx 0$
  **mechanically**. Running global CD on two-way FE residuals and reading
  non-rejection as "no dependence" is an artefact of the transformation, not
  evidence [@croissant2019, §10.1.2.2].

The general statement of that second point is @juodis2022: with period-specific
parameters *estimated* rather than known, CD **diverges as T grows even when
the dependence has been correctly accounted for**. It is an incidental
parameters problem, and it applies to CCE residuals as much as to two-way FE
residuals. This is the trap in §8's defactor-then-re-diagnose sequence: the
obvious diagnostic at step 3 is exactly the one that is invalid there. On
US house prices, two-way FE moves $\overline{\lvert\rho\rvert}$ only from 0.51
to 0.49 while collapsing CD from 53.3 to 0.02, p = 0.98 — see
[testing for CSD](../panel-spat.qmd#sec-csd-tests).

**And its null is not independence.** The implicit null of CD is *weak*
dependence — α < 1/4 when *N* and *T* grow at the same rate
[@pesaran2015weak; @pesaran2015, p. 786]. Confirmed from the other direction at
[@pesaran2015, p. 839], where CD is found to be the statistic *most robust to*
spatial alternatives — which is to say, **it does not fire on them.**

::: {.callout-warning}
**CD is a one-bit read on α, and a coarse one.** Its size is only assured below
α ≈ 1/4; the statistic starts diverging somewhere above α ≈ 1/2. In between there
is a band where it is neither reliably valid nor reliably powerful. Do not read a
CD rejection as "there is dependence"; read it as "there is *pervasive*
dependence".
:::

## 5. The LM family: which one, and when

All available through `plm::pcdtest(test = ...)`.

| `test =` | Statistic | Use it when | Watch out |
|---|---|---|---|
| `"cd"` | Pesaran CD, eq. 29.76 | Large *N*, small *T*; the default first look | Dies on demeaned residuals; blind to sign cancellation |
| `"lm"` | Breusch–Pagan LM, eq. 13.32 [@baltagi2021, p. 412] | $T \gg N$ only | Diverges with large *N*; poorly centred at finite *T* |
| `"sclm"` | Scaled LM | Slightly larger *N* than `"lm"` tolerates | Still badly centred at finite *T*: **14.25% rejection at N=200, T=20 against a nominal 5%** [@pesaran2015, p. 789] |
| `"bcsclm"` | Bias-corrected scaled LM, eq. 13.36 [@baltagi2012; @baltagi2021, p. 414] | **The FE-appropriate one** | Requires a `within` model with individual or two-way effects |
| `"rho"`, `"absrho"` | $\bar\rho$ and $\overline{\lvert\rho\rvert}$ | Always — see §6 | Not tests; no null, no p-value |

If you are testing residuals from a fixed-effects model, `"bcsclm"` is the answer
and the others are history. It exists precisely because the scaled LM's finite-*T*
bias, quantified above, makes it unusable at the *N* and *T* that panels
actually have.

### What `plm` does not have

Three later statistics attack CD's blindness from different directions. None is
in `plm`; all three are in `dcce::pcd_test` [@wasseja2026].

| `test =` | Statistic | What it changes | Watch out |
|---|---|---|---|
| `"cdw"` | Weighted CD [@juodis2022] | Rademacher weights, so estimated period-specific parameters cannot make CD diverge | Buys size with power: it fails to reject even on raw series with $\bar\rho = 0.29$. Seed-dependent |
| `"pea"` | Power-enhanced [@fan2015] | Adds a screening term that fires on sparse alternatives | Enormous statistics; read it as a flag, not a magnitude |
| `"cdstar"` | Bias-corrected CD\* [@pesaran2021cd] | A PCA correction valid whether latent factors are weak or strong | Needs the factor count `n_pca`; the default is 1 |

**CD\* is the one to reach for at step 3 of §8.** It keeps power where CDw
loses it and stays valid where plain CD does not.

## 6. ρ̄ versus |ρ̄|: the poor man's α

The last row of that table is the most useful and the most ignored. `"rho"` gives
you $\bar\rho$; `"absrho"` gives you $\overline{\lvert\rho\rvert}$. Two numbers,
no null hypothesis, and together they diagnose the exact failure mode of the test
sitting next to them:

| Pattern | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| $\bar\rho \approx \overline{\lvert\rho\rvert}$, both large | Pervasive, same-signed co-movement | You are near α = 1. Factor structure. Go to CCE. |
| $\bar\rho \approx 0$, $\overline{\lvert\rho\rvert}$ large | Real dependence that **cancels in sign** | CD is blind here by construction. Go to the [ordered tests](03-spatial-dependence-tests.qmd). |
| both small | Little dependence of any kind | Low α. FE plus an honest vcov. |

The middle row is the case where CD reports nothing and something is nonetheless
badly wrong. Compute both; they cost nothing.

## 7. If / then

| If | Then |
|---|---|
| α ≈ 1, or $\bar\rho \approx \overline{\lvert\rho\rvert}$ and large | Strong dependence. **CCE** [@pesaran2006]. FE is biased, not just inefficient. |
| α clearly below 1 and CD does not fire | Weak dependence. FE is consistent — now ask whether it is *spatial* ([note 03](03-spatial-dependence-tests.qmd)). |
| α in the 0.8–0.95 middle | **The modal case.** Defactor first, then re-diagnose. See §8. |
| $\bar\rho \approx 0$ but $\overline{\lvert\rho\rvert}$ large | Sign cancellation. Ignore CD entirely; use the ordered tests. |
| You only have two-way FE residuals | Global CD is uninformative by construction. Use `"bcsclm"`, CD\* [@pesaran2021cd], or the randomised-W test [@millo2017]. |
| You have defactored (CCE, PC) residuals | Same problem, general form [@juodis2022]. CD\* or CDw, never plain CD. |
| Dependence confirmed, structure unknown | Do **not** route on α alone. Corroborate with the `rwtest` vs `pcdtest` contrast (plan §5.7). |

## 8. The middle is the normal case

Given that most real panels sit around α ≈ 0.8–0.95, the weak/strong fork is not
usually a fork at all. It is a **sequence**, and @bailey2016 apply it that way —
estimating α on the raw series *and* on residuals after removing factors:

1. Estimate α (or read $\bar\rho$ vs $\overline{\lvert\rho\rvert}$) on the raw
   series — `csd_exp(use_residuals = FALSE)`, the @bailey2016 variable method.
2. If it points strong → **defactor** (CCE, or principal components).
3. Re-diagnose the residuals with `csd_exp(use_residuals = TRUE)`, the
   @bailey2019 residual method, which is built for exactly this step. If α has
   dropped toward 1/2, the remaining dependence is local, and *now* modelling
   it spatially is legitimate. Do **not** use plain CD here — see @juodis2022
   in §4; use CD\*.

Run on US house prices, the sequence gives α = 0.83 on the raw series and
α = 0.51 on the CCEMG residuals, which is the clean version of this picture:
[the exponent α](../panel-spat.qmd#sec-csd-exponent).

Fitting a spatial model to data with an unremoved common factor gets you a
significant $\hat\rho$ that is picking up the factor, not the geography. That is
the single most common way this goes wrong.

## 9. Open

- **An implementation now exists, and it is young.** `dcce::csd_exp`
  [@wasseja2026] implements both the @bailey2016 variable method and the
  @bailey2019 residual method, and it reproduces its own vignette's
  α = 0.8348 for `pwt8` exactly. But **dcce** is a single-author package first
  published in 2026 with no independent validation, so the α numbers here rest
  on one cross-check: its Pesaran CD agrees with `plm::pcdtest` to four
  decimals on the same data. Corroborate α with the `rwtest` vs `pcdtest`
  contrast (plan §5.7) rather than routing on it alone.
- **The variable method is fragile in exactly the way the theory predicts.**
  It inverts $\hat\alpha = 1 + \ln(\hat\sigma^2_{\bar z}) / (2\ln N)$ with a
  correction for the $\kappa_1 N^{-1}$ term, and that correction scales as
  $\overline{\sigma^2_i} / (2 \ln N \cdot \widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\bar
  z_t))$. When the common component does not survive averaging, the correction
  dominates and the estimate leaves the parameter space entirely — below 1/2 on
  house prices, and large and negative on an independent panel. That is the
  callout in §1 made visible: there really is nothing to measure down there.
  The package does not constrain the output to (1/2, 1], so check the number
  against $\bar\rho$ before believing it.
- **The 1/4-to-1/2 band.** The size condition α < 1/4 [@pesaran2015, p. 786] and
  the point at which CD starts diverging are different quantities, and the gap
  between them is not well characterised here. Check against @pesaran2015weak
  before relying on it.
